admin.title: Trainer Administration
admin.subtitle: Maintain users, assign roles, reset passwords, and monitor system metrics.
admin.instanceHint: If this app runs behind a reverse proxy, the browser's own address may not be the one others should use to reach a collection share link. Set the public URL here to override it. Leave blank to use the browser's address (or the {envVar} environment variable, if set).
admin.pokemonProviderHint: Where English Pokémon cards and sets come from. New installs start on TCGdex; an install upgraded from an older version keeps pokemontcg.io, because its cached cards are numbered by it. Non-English always uses TCGdex, which is the only provider that carries other languages. TCGdex is also faster and needs no API key (measured: 66-83ms per card lookup against pokemontcg.io's 971-1963ms, which also answers 5xx often enough to need retries). The two number the same sets differently, so switching re-downloads the set list and rebuilds the TCGplayer product map — cards already cached under the old numbering stay, and are still searchable.
admin.setIndexHint: Per-set image indexes power set-scoped camera scanning. They build automatically the first time a set is scanned; build them here ahead of time, or remove ones you no longer need. Use the MTG set code (e.g. mh3) or Pokémon set id (e.g. sv1).
admin.previewSummary: {count} printings, up to {size} on disk. Downloads one image per card; can take several minutes.
admin.globalHint: Whole-game image indexes power scanning when no set is selected. Rebuilding pulls every card (both faces of double-faced cards), so newly released sets and card backs become scannable. This is heavy: tens of thousands of images, the CLIP model on CPU, ~1GB on disk, and can run for hours. The existing index keeps serving scans until a rebuild finishes, and a stopped or failed build can be resumed instead of restarted.
admin.globalDerivedHint: These are built from the per-set indexes below: one walk over every set downloads each card image once and produces both a recall table and the feature index. Indexing every set is the same job without the whole-game tables.
admin.preflightOk: Preflight passed — card source, images and encoder all reachable ({sets} sets listed).
admin.addGlobalLangHint: Each language is a separate multi-hour build (~1.6GB). Build only the languages you collect.
admin.removeGlobalLang: Remove this language from the list
admin.backupHint: Writes a consistent snapshot of the entire database (users, collections, decks, settings) to a file on the server. The newest {keep} are kept. Download one to keep it off-server. To restore: stop the server, replace {dbFile} with a backup file, and restart.

A catalog built on this install is keyed by your own cards, which makes the same lookup instant. An admin can build one for the sets you own in Admin → Scan catalogs; a few sets takes minutes.

setup.language.title: Welcome, {name}.
setup.language.sub: Bindarr tracks a card collection: what you own, what it is worth, and where each card is stored. Everything runs on this server.
setup.language.body: This sets up the parts that need a decision from you: your language, which cards you collect, the scanner, and optional API keys. All of it can be changed later in Settings and Admin.

setup.scan.title: Card scanning
setup.scan.sub: Scanning identifies a card from your camera. It needs two model files to read the image, and a catalog to compare it against. Without both, the scanner stays off and you add cards by search instead.
setup.scan.recogniserBody: Finds the card in the frame and turns it into something comparable. Licensed {license}, which is why they are downloaded on request rather than shipped with Bindarr (MIT).
setup.scan.catalogBody: A prebuilt catalog of card images to match against. It is a fixed snapshot, so cards printed after its date are not in it.
setup.scan.needModels: Download the recogniser first. A catalog is unusable without it.
setup.scan.buildHint: Admin → Catalogs can also build a catalog here from the sets you own. That stays current as new sets release, and takes minutes per set.
setup.scan.buildHintBuilt: This install already has one built.
setup.keys.title: API keys
setup.keys.sub: All three are optional and free. Bindarr works without them. They are also in Settings if you would rather do this later.
setup.keys.tcgBody: Raises the search rate limit from {from} to {to} requests a day, which matters during bulk scanning.
setup.keys.psaBody: Typing a cert number fills in the card and its grade instead of you entering both.
setup.keys.gradedBody: Prices a slab at what that grade sells for, instead of falling back to the raw card price. Pokémon only.
setup.tour.title: What each tab does
setup.tour.addCards: Scan with a camera, search by name, or paste a list. You confirm the printing and condition, and it is added to your collection.
setup.tour.collection: Everything you own, filtered by set, tag, condition or value. Click a card for price history, grading and notes.
setup.tour.decks: Build decks from cards you own. Checking a deck out tells you which page each card came from; checking it in puts them back.
setup.tour.dashboard: Dashboard is collection value over time and recent activity. Notes is a scratchpad for trades and wants.
setup.tour.settings: Settings holds your password, API keys, theme and share link. Admin holds users, catalogs, price sweeps and backups. Everything in this wizard is in one of those two.

catalog.title: Scan Catalogs
catalog.intro: Two downloads get the scanner working. Building your own catalog is optional, and worth it once you want the sets you actually own to stay current.
catalog.engineDesc: Two model files ({size}) that find the card in frame and recognise it. Scanning does nothing without them.
catalog.engineLicense: {spdx} — not bundled with Bindarr (MIT). Downloading them into your own install is your call.
catalog.readyMadeDesc: Precomputed by the model's author. Each is a snapshot: cards printed after its date are missing, it can never be updated, and it cannot be counted per set. A catalog you build in step 3 always takes precedence over it.
catalog.magicVsPokemon: Magic stores Scryfall ids, so a scan fetches whatever card it matched — nothing else needed. Pokémon stores TCGplayer product ids, which name a card only through the product map below. Getting the catalog builds that map automatically; without it a Pokémon scan matches and then names nothing.
catalog.engineRequiredNote: A catalog on its own cannot scan — install the scan engine above too.
catalog.productMapDesc: What turns a TCGplayer product id into a set and a card number, so a Pokémon match can be looked up and cached like any search. One request per set from tcgcsv.com, a few hundred in total. Refresh it after new sets release; Magic does not use it.
catalog.errListSets: Could not load the set list
catalog.setsSelected.one: {count} set code selected — adds to what is already built.
catalog.setsSelected.other: {count} set codes selected — adds to what is already built.
catalog.setsSelectHint: Tick the sets you own — those are the ones a scan has to answer. Subsets (tokens, promos) come with their parent, and each build adds to the last.
catalog.searchMtgPlaceholder: Search sets, e.g. Foundations or FDN
catalog.otherLangsDesc: Pokémon only. Magic needs no per-language catalog: the scanner matches artwork, and a localized Magic printing is the same set with the same illustration — so the English catalog already identifies a Japanese card and the scan result is re-expressed by set and number. (Japanese-exclusive alternate art, like the War of the Spark planeswalkers, is the one exception, and it is a few hundred cards.) Japanese Pokémon is the opposite case: whole sets that never released in English, which nothing in the English catalog can match.
catalog.errLanguageList: Could not load the language list: {error}
catalog.askingProvider: Asking the provider what it publishes…
catalog.cardsIndexableDesc: “Cards we can index” counts the cards this install has downloaded WITH artwork, against every card the provider lists for that language. It never reaches 100%: TCGdex lists 177 Japanese sets and holds card records for 28 of them, so the rest can be listed but not fetched. Build a language and the left number is what the scanner will search.
catalog.noOtherLanguages: The provider publishes nothing in any other language right now.
catalog.errStartProductMapGeneric: Could not start the product map build

catalog.newSetsWarning.one: {count} set not downloaded yet — cards from it will be misidentified. Build to add it; any the provider has no data for are skipped and stop being counted.
catalog.newSetsWarning.other: {count} sets not downloaded yet — cards from them will be misidentified. Build to add them; any the provider has no data for are skipped and stop being counted.
catalog.buildYourOwnDesc: Open a game to pick sets. Every match resolves to a card you hold, new sets can be added as they release, and each build merges into the last — so a few sets at a time is the point, not a compromise. Builds resume, and stopping keeps everything built so far.
catalog.speedTitle: It also makes scanning much faster.
catalog.speedDesc: A ready-made catalog identifies cards by a provider id, so the first scan of any card has to fetch it from that provider before it can be shown — measured 971-1963 ms for Pokémon and 164 ms for Magic, per card. A locally built catalog is keyed by this install's own card ids, so the same lookup is a database read: about 1 ms, with no provider call and nothing to fail. Building only the sets you own is enough to get that for the cards you actually scan.
